In this lesson you will learn about the careers, history and professional certifications associated with aircraft maintenance.
The definition of an aircraft includes any form of craft designed for flight through or navigation in the air; as airplanes, blimps, balloons, helicopters and gliders.ers.
Keeping those aircraft in flight-ready condition is the job of the Aviation Maintenance Technician and the Avionics Technician.

These technicians work on sophisticated aircraft systems, components, and equipment to ensure that every flight begins and ends successfully. Unlike many other careers, in aviation maintenance, there is no room for error. There is no "second chance" to get the job right...

But, at the same time, an aviation maintenance career can be very rewarding. Getting a multi-million dollar, state-of-the-art aircraft in the air after it has come to you with a malfunction is an art form in itself.

Every school child knows how aviation began. Two brothers from Ohio lugged a 600 pound craft across the sands of Kitty Hawk, North Carolina and became the first humans to accomplish controlled, sustained flight in a heavier-than-air craft from level ground...

If the Wright Brothers were renowned as the world's first pilots, then Charles Taylor must be considered the world's first Aviation Maintenance Technician. He worked for the Wrights in their Dayton bicycle shop as a mechanic. When the brothers could not find a light weight engine to purchase for their flyer, they turned to Taylor to build one...

Charles Taylor went to work and built a four-cylinder, gasoline powered engine that was lightweight and powerful enough to turn two large propellers. He actually hand-tooled the engine's crankshaft on the bicycle shop lathe...

Taylor's engine was quite crude by today's standards. It did not have a carburetor; instead, it dumped raw gas into the cylinders. Its oil system was just a pan of oil that was splashed up onto the rotating parts. In Charles Taylor's own words, "It weren't much of an engine".
Charles Taylor's simple engine had a power to weight ratio that was better than any other engine of its day. It lifted the Wright Flyer into the air and into history.
World War I was the first war to see aerial battles. Planes were made out of wood and fabric, so some of the best military aircraft mechanics were wood craftsman.

Following WWI, the government sold surplus aircraft to ex-military aviators. These pilots became the barnstormers of the early 1920's who introduced flying to America. At that time, there were no government regulations on flying or maintaining aircraft, so, for the most part, barnstormers repaired their own planes.

By the mid 1920s, more and more people were taking to the sky. The Federal government began to control the skies by certifying airplanes and airman. WWI aircraft were disappearing and manufacturers began to emerge that built only aircraft.
One such manufacturer was Ryan Airlines, Inc. in San Diego. Ryan had been building the M-1 and M-2 high-wing monoplanes for the mail service for many years.

In 1927, Ryan Airlines received an interesting request from a St. Louis based mail pilot. Could Ryan build him an aircraft that could fly from New York to Paris... And construct it in 3 months? We all know the answer to that question!!!
On May 20, 1927, Charles Lindbergh took off in his Ryan-built "Spirit of St. Louis" from Roosevelt field on Long Island for the first successful non-stop trans-Atlantic flight.

So, why was this event significant to Aviation Maintenance History? The Spirit of St. Louis was a significantly modified Ryan M-2. The mechanic that fabricated and installed these modifications was none other than Douglas Corrigan, better known as "Wrong-Way Corrigan".....
Douglas Corrigan was a young but talented mechanic at Ryan Airlines, Inc. He was key to making the modifications that allowed the Spirit of St. Louis to fly for over 36 hours non-stop.

Unfortunately, Douglas Corrigan is better known for his disregard of aviation regulations than for constructing a record breaking aircraft. Corrigan was so inspired by Lindbergh's trans-Atlantic flight the he wanted to be the first to fly from New York to Dublin, Ireland. He learned to fly, purchased a Curtiss Robin airplane for $325, and began his planning....

Before WWII however, women were already making their mark in Aviation Maintenance History. One such woman was Phoebe Fairgrave Omlie.
Phoebe Omlie began her aviation career as a barnstormer, flying circus performer/owner, and silent motion picture stunt women. Soon she learned to fly the aircraft she bought for her circus.
Since aircraft mechanics were a rare find at the remote fields her circus performed at, in 1927, Phoebe became the first female to earn a aircraft mechanic license. she bought for her circus.

By maintaining her own aircraft, she didn't need to carry a mechanic on any of her long distance flights. This action squashed rumors that male mechanics actually flew the record setting flights for women aviators..

Following WWII, there were tremendous advances in aviation. In 1943, Germany developed a jet fighter which could reach speeds of 500 MPH in level flight. This brought to aviation a new breed of maintenance technicians, the "jet mechanics"...

Today, the Space Shuttle can circumnavigate the earth in 90 minutes; over 30 hours less than it took Lindbergh to fly from New York to Paris. The technicians that keep these aircraft flying are trained in advance systems, engines, and airframe techniques.

The future of public transportation is already taking shape with the development of aerospace vehicles. These vehicles will be using low-earth orbit technology to reach any destination around the globe in less than an hour. These very sophisticated aircraft with very sophisticated systems will be maintained by well trained technicians. Technicians like you!!!!!

The Federal Aviation Administration, under the United States Department of Transportation, provides regulatory control over the aviation industry through the Federal Aviation Regulations or FAR's.
The FAR's are designed to provide guidance and rules to ensure that aircraft and airspace are safe for all of us.

As an Aviation Maintenance Technician, you will be regulated under several parts of the FAR's. FAR Parts 65, 145, and 147 each describe and mandate regulations in the certification process of aircraft technicians...

FAR Part 145 states that any U.S. company requesting a repair station certification must provide adequate personnel who are certified as either a mechanic or repairman under FAR Part 65. Basically, all airport FBO's, airline repair facilities, manufacturing, or overhaul facilities must have certified mechanics working for them in order to operate.....

The FAA requires certain technicians to be certified in the aircraft industry to maintain high standards and safety consciousness. The guidelines and regulations for aircraft maintenance technician certifications are found in the FAR Part 65.

Currently, there are two mechanic ratings: Airframe and Powerplant. To be eligible for a mechanic certificate, a person must be at least 18 years of age, have passed all of the prescribed written, oral, and practical tests within a 24 month period, and satisfy the requirements for the applicable rating.

The Airframe rating certifies the mechanic to work on aircraft structures, systems, and components. The Powerplant rating certifies the mechanic to work on engines and propellers. It is typical for technicians to hold both ratings as an A&P Mechanic.

To be eligible to take the exams, an applicant must provide documentary evidence of eligibility in one of three ways. The first way is with an appropriate graduation certificate or certificate of completion from an FAA certified aviation maintenance technician school. Rules and regulations for certifying aviation maintenance schools are found in FAR Part 147....

If the applicant has not been to a formal aviation school, they must provide documentary evidence of at least 18 months of practical experience with the procedures, practices, materials, tools, and equipment used in constructing, maintaining, or altering airframes, or powerplants appropriate to the rating sought.
Or at least 30 months of practical experience concurrently performing the duties appropriate to both the airframe and powerplant ratings..

Regardless of where the applicant gained experience in aircraft maintenance, a school or hands-on, each applicant must pass the written, oral, and practical tests with a minimum of 70%. The practical tests consist of projects and tasks covered by the written and oral tests.

One advantage of attending a certified aviation maintenance school is that FAR Part 65 allows students to take the oral and practical tests as part of their normal curriculum before passing the FAA written exam. This is very convenient since most certified schools have examiners on campus.

Avionics Technicians usually work in one of three areas: flight line maintenance, installation and manufacturing, or the electronics shop. None of these positions require certification. Avionics technicians only need Federal Communications Commission (FCC) certifications are if they work on transmitters above a certain power or on radar systems.

Once you get an FAA certification as an Aviation Maintenance Technician or an FCC certification as an Avionics Technician, the certificates are good indefinitely unless revoked. There are minimum requirements for working on types of aircraft; however, once certified, it stays with you forever.

Another method of certification through the FAA is the Repairman Certificate. The certificate is designed to assist large maintenance operations, manufacturing plants, and overhaul facilities in certifying their workers. Instead of being certified in the many skills required by an A&P technician, the Repairman is certified in specific skills on specific aircraft.aircraft.. aircraft.

To get certified as a Repairman, you must have been on the job at the company for a minimum of 18 months actually performing the tasks that are being certified. If you leave the company, or change job skills, your certification is no longer valid.
Many companies use the Repairman certificate to manage their manufacturing and line maintenance Avionics needs as well as certifying mechanics to specific areas.
